newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Choppy trade seen ahead of jobs.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Choppy trade seen ahead of jobs.

text.p: Choppy trade was expected Tuesday in the U.S. Treasuries market, with little significant data slated ahead of Friday's nonfarm payrolls report.

Leading economic indicators were scheduled for release at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, but analysts said the figures were not likely to have much impact on bond prices. The BTM/Schroders and Redbook readings also were due, giving a glimpse on consumer spending patterns.
But, traders said, no substantial price movement was expected before the payrolls report.

Brian Jones, economist at Salomon Brothers Inc, predicted the chain store numbers would be a bit stronger but forecast growth of 300,000 in nonfarm payrolls despite the Bureau of Labor Statistics seasonal revisions -- changes which have prompted many economists to lower their estimates of job growth by as much as 100,000 for the month.
Economists polled by Reuters expected, on average, that payrolls would rise 221,000 in May.
Jones said the weather during the survey period in April was miserable and a bounceback was inevitable as construction and amusement jobs would materialize.
Jones said the seasonal adjustments "were like sitting on a water bed. Sit on one side and the other will go up."
He saw the Federal Reserve ratcheting short-term interest rates up 25 basis points at its July policy-making meeting and by 75 basis points before the end of the year.

The Fed last raised interest rates at its FOMC meeting on March 25, but paused at its meeting on May 20. While the Fed has never moved to tighten or ease monetary policy only once in either direction under Chairman Alan Greenspan, analysts argued that currently there was leeway to do so as the spread between the fed funds and real interest rates was low.

John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co, said that with the lack of supply and data releases the market likely would remain on hold until payrolls came out on Friday. He saw nonfarm payrolls rising by 215,000.
"Things got confused since the adjustments (by the BLS last Friday), but the economy remains strong with output and employment outperforming consumer spending," Ryding said.

Ryding said yields at the long end of the maturity spectrum were probably at the high end of near-term ranges and could possibly get back to 7.0 percent, but not much further. He saw one more tightening by the Fed, then a neutral stance.
"I suspect that for a good portion of this week people are going to be thinking about the employment report and not doing a lot," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
The BTM/Schroders and Redbook indices could have some effect on the market as strength in household spending would be a surprise following a robust first quarter, Moran said.

He saw nonfarm payrolls rising by 225,000 in May and said the number would be pivotal for Fed policymakers. "Right now, I'm slightly leaning for them to do nothing (in July), but that would change with strong reports," Moran said.
The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee next meets on July 1 and 2.

Treasuries continued to glean support from developments in Europe on Monday. French voters elected Socialist Lionel Jospin prime minister on Sunday, meaning President Jacques Chirac would have to share power with the left wing. That prospect spooked many investors, fearful that the fiscal policy reform seen under the center-right government would unravel.
